analysis.one_liner: Bans persistent toxic pollutants and sets rules for adding new chemicals under three international toxics treaties.
analysis.headline: The House Energy and Commerce Committee approved the bill twice in 2006 — by votes of 15-10 and 28-15 — but it never reached the House floor before the Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write three international agreements on dangerous 'persistent organic pollutants' — chemicals like DDT and PCBs that stay in the environment and build up in people and wildlife — into U.S. law. It outright bans manufacture, use, and export of a listed set of these chemicals, and sets up a public notice-and-comment process when international treaty bodies propose adding a new chemical. For any new chemical, the EPA could only issue protections after the United States formally ratifies the treaty amendment, and the EPA would have to balance health risks against economic costs. The bill also requires exporters of banned or restricted chemicals to notify the government and importing countries first.
analysis.who_benefits: People exposed to persistent toxic chemicals — through contaminated food, water, air, or old equipment — would gain long-term health protections, since these chemicals accumulate in bodies and the environment for decades. Americans would also gain notice about hazardous chemicals being shipped abroad. Foreign countries that import U.S. chemicals would get formal warning labels and safety information on banned or severely restricted chemicals.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People exposed to long-lasting toxic chemicals

how_it_helps.text: The bill outright prohibits the manufacture, processing, export, use, and disposal of named persistent organic pollutants, including DDT, chlordane, and PCBs, with narrow exceptions [S3].

When international treaty committees propose adding a new chemical to the banned list, the EPA must publish a notice within 60 days and open it for public comment, giving citizens a window into the process [S3].

Exporters of banned or severely restricted chemicals must give advance notice before each export, label the chemicals with hazard information, and attach safety data sheets, so importing countries know what they are receiving [S3].
The bill tightens PCB rules, barring export of equipment — like transformers and capacitors — containing more than trace amounts of PCB liquids, except for environmentally sound waste disposal [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers and pesticide producers would bear the cost of prohibitions on listed chemicals and the paperwork of the new-chemical review process. Chemical and equipment exporters would bear the cost of pre-export notices, labeling, and conditions on shipments. If a new chemical is restricted and no substitute exists, users of that chemical — including farmers and industrial processors — could face higher costs or supply disruptions.

drawbacks.text: For chemicals added to the treaties in the future, no EPA rule can take effect until the United States ratifies the amendment, and the bill states Congress's view that the U.S. should only ratify after formally declaring that each amendment takes effect upon ratification — meaning each new listing requires a separate act of political will [S3].

The EPA must weigh economic consequences, effects on small business, and technological innovation when regulating a newly listed chemical, and must balance 'social, environmental, and economic costs and benefits' — language that lets economics soften health protections [S3].
Regulations on newly listed chemicals face judicial review under a 'substantial evidence' standard, a stricter legal test that makes rules easier to overturn in court [S3].

The bill carves out exemptions that keep some uses legal, including lindane for seed treatment and public health, closed-system chemical intermediates, and exports of still-permitted toxic chemicals to countries that are not parties to the treaty, provided they file annual certifications [S3].

Conforming amendments would bar states from keeping chemical protections that differ from federal rules once the U.S. consents to a treaty provision, unless state rules are identical to the federal requirement [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The immediate bans on already-named toxic chemicals are real and low-risk, since nearly all of them are long banned or tightly controlled in the U.S. already. But the bill's design deliberately slows protection against future chemicals: ratification gatekeeping, mandatory cost-benefit balancing, strict judicial review, and state preemption all trade speed and strength of regulation for predictability for chemical producers. A supporter would call that balance prudent; a critic would call it a mechanism that lets a future administration or a handful of senators indefinitely block any new chemical from being restricted.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared its House committee in November 2006 and was placed on the House calendar, but the session ended in early January 2007 without the House ever voting on it, and the Senate never took it up.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Gillmor introduced the bill on December 16, 2005, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee [S6].
The Environment and Hazardous Materials Subcommittee ordered the bill reported on May 18, 2006, by a vote of 15-10 [S6].
The full committee ordered the bill reported on July 12, 2006, by a vote of 28-15 [S6].
The committee formally reported the amended bill on November 15, 2006, as House Report 109-714, and it was placed on the Union Calendar, the list of bills awaiting House floor action [S6].
The bill received no House floor vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and the Senate never considered it [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical manufacturers and exporters came out ahead: the treaty-implementation regime never took effect, and the United States still has not joined the Stockholm Convention, so the U.S. chemical industry faces no new treaty-based restrictions from this effort. Anyone hoping for stronger U.S. participation in the international toxics regime gained nothing.

industries.note: The bill bans a list of already-controlled toxic chemicals, but it also locks in an industry-favored architecture for any future regulation: new chemical listings cannot take effect without U.S. ratification, the EPA must weigh economic costs against health, and rules face strict 'substantial evidence' court review. That structure makes the chemical industry's economic position a permanent, built-in factor in every future toxics decision.

Exporters of banned or severely restricted chemicals would face advance notice requirements, labeling, safety documentation, and export conditions, and PCB-contaminated equipment could no longer be exported except for sound disposal. These are compliance costs, but they exist to warn foreign buyers and protect health abroad.

The bill preserves lindane and technical HCH uses for seed treatment and public health under the LRTAP protocol, keeping certain pesticide options open, while other listed pesticides remain banned. Farmers and health programs keep some tools that a stricter implementation might have removed.
